headline: Questions on Apple's Investigatory Powers Tribunal proceedings, data-centre water and energy requirements, and a published government response on human rights and AI feature alongside Capita pension delays and public-sector AI procurement scrutiny.
summary: MPs and peers asked about Capita's pension-scheme delays, data-centre environmental impacts and community benefits, and public-sector AI procurement standards. The evidence also records questions about Apple's tribunal proceedings and a publication titled "Human Rights and the Regulation of AI: Government Response". The supplied written questions and answers do not directly name Microsoft, Google, Amazon/AWS, OpenAI or Anthropic.

very_important.title: MP asks Home Office about Apple's tribunal proceedings and technical capability notices
very_important.body: Rupert Lowe tabled three written questions on 20 November 2026. He asked about legal costs in Apple's Investigatory Powers Tribunal proceedings concerning a technical capability notice, annual numbers of notices issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, and review of the policy of neither confirming nor denying their existence. The third question referred to a tribunal ruling dated 19 November 2026. No answers to these questions are recorded in the evidence.
very_important.why: These questions concern legal costs, surveillance powers and transparency about technical capability notices. The evidence does not supply the ruling or establish its outcome or precedential effect.

very_important.title: Commons and Lords questions on departmental engagement with GDS, the Government Cyber Unit and NCSC on AI procurement
very_important.where: Commons and Lords written questions, DCMS
very_important.body: Dr Ben Spencer and Viscount Camrose asked near-identical questions on which departments have engaged the Government Digital Service, Government Cyber Unit and National Cyber Security Centre on AI procurement. The government confirmed AI procurement is subject to the AI Playbook, Government Cyber Unit security requirements, NCSC guidance, Secure by Design principles, the AI Cyber Security Code of Practice and international standard EN 304 223, but said individual procurement decisions remain for organisations within existing frameworks.
very_important.why: Relevant to security and governance controls for public-sector AI procurement.
very_important.linkText: Dr Ben Spencer, Artificial Intelligence: Procurement, UIN 38195

very_important.title: Government response to report on human rights and AI regulation published
very_important.body: The publication "2nd Special Report - Human Rights and the Regulation of AI: Government Response" was published on 20 November 2026.
very_important.why: Records publication of a government response concerning human rights and AI regulation; the response's contents are not supplied.
very_important.linkText: 2nd Special Report - Human Rights and the Regulation of AI: Government Response

very_important.title: Slough MP asks about data-centre water, energy and community benefits
very_important.where: Commons written questions, Department for Energy Security and Net Zero / Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
very_important.body: Mr Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi, MP for Slough, asked about water and energy impact assessments, the local water, temperature, biodiversity and electricity impacts of multiple data-centre developments, and monitoring and enforcement of the Data Centre Covenant's community-benefit requirements. In answers to UINs 43026 and 43027, Martin McCluskey referred to the Written Ministerial Statement on "Enabling Sustainable Data Centre Growth Through Responsible Water and Energy Use". He said strategic data centres will have to report annually on water and energy use, efficiency, emissions and heat reuse. All new data centres are encouraged to meet Covenant tests; strategically important centres seeking enhanced government support will be required to meet them. No answer to the community-benefit enforcement question, UIN 45176, is recorded.
very_important.why: Concerns data-centre resource use, environmental impacts and community-benefit requirements.
very_important.linkText: Mr Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi, Energy and Water: Data Centres, UIN 43026

very_important.title: Cabinet Office says Capita missed 'multiple critical milestones' and £9.9m has been withheld
very_important.body: Euan Stainbank and Bill Esterson separately asked about Capita's administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme. The Cabinet Office said multiple critical milestones were missed across 12 contractually defined transition phases, £9.9 million in contract payments has been withheld, and officials are working with Capita on a "five-workstream recovery plan" while shaping a long-term strategy to bring the scheme back in-house. It said no financial penalties have been imposed beyond the withheld amount.
very_important.why: Relevant to supplier accountability, contract management and plans to bring pension administration back in-house.

questions.title: Calls to pause GOV.UK One Login rollout and guarantee non-digital alternatives
questions.body: Rupert Lowe asked about the merits of a statutory right to a free non-digital alternative for identity verification. Sorcha Eastwood asked whether additional GOV.UK One Login onboarding would be paused pending independent review and whether free, genuinely equivalent non-digital alternatives would receive a statutory guarantee. The government said One Login is not mandatory, alternative routes are decided by the relevant service, and rollout will continue. It described departmental controls, HM Treasury oversight, independent assurance by NISTA and independent assurance and certification under the UK Digital Verification Services Trust Framework.
questions.why: Concerns continued rollout and alternatives for people who cannot or do not wish to use One Login.
questions.linkText: Rupert Lowe, Electronic Government: Proof of Identity, UIN 39385

questions.title: Questions on whether GOV.UK One Login meets NCSC cyber standards
questions.who: Martin Wrigley (Liberal Democrat); Anna Sabine (Liberal Democrat)
questions.body: Martin Wrigley asked about alternative routes and dedicated troubleshooting teams for people unable to confirm their identity through the listed verification routes. The government pointed to service-specific alternatives and its Customer Contact Centre. Anna Sabine asked whether One Login is fully aligned with NCSC's Cyber Assessment Framework. Her answer said the programme follows CAF security standards and receives independent testing and NCSC advice, but did not disclose operational security specifics.
questions.why: Concerns accessibility and cyber assurance of government digital identity services.
questions.linkText: Anna Sabine, Electronic Government: Cybersecurity, UIN 42906

questions.title: Question on whether the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum should get statutory AI powers
questions.body: Dr Ben Spencer asked about the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum's budget, staffing and whether the government intends to give it a statutory AI function. The answer described a voluntary forum of the Competition and Markets Authority, Ofcom, Information Commission and Financial Conduct Authority, not overseen by government. It did not state whether a statutory AI function would be introduced.
questions.why: Raises the question of statutory AI responsibilities; the answer does not establish the government's intentions.
questions.linkText: Dr Ben Spencer, Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum, UIN 30880

questions.title: Shadow Defence Minister presses MOD on AI investment and autonomous-weapons risk
questions.where: Commons written questions, Ministry of Defence
questions.body: Stuart Anderson tabled eight written questions on 20 November 2026 about defence AI investment since the Defence Investment Plan, capabilities expected to incorporate AI before 2030, current AI-enabled projects, autonomous-weapons opportunities and risks, AI decision-support tools, emerging-technology research funding, accelerating adoption of new technologies, and progress implementing Strategic Defence Review recommendations on science, technology and innovation. No answers are recorded in the evidence.
questions.why: Concerns defence AI investment, implementation and autonomous-weapons risks.
questions.linkText: Stuart Anderson, Defence: Artificial Intelligence, UIN 45198

questions.title: Peer presses for safeguards on AI companion toys and chatbots marketed to children
questions.where: Lords written questions, Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade / DCMS / Department for Education
questions.body: Baroness Benjamin asked whether government will use Product Regulation and Metrology Act 2025 powers to prohibit generative-AI chatbot toys for under-16s pending independent testing, what evidence exists that AI companion toys benefit children's emotional development, and what guidance has gone to early-years settings on AI-enabled toys. No answers are recorded in the evidence.
questions.why: Concerns testing, developmental claims and guidance for AI-enabled toys used by children.
questions.linkText: Baroness Benjamin, Toys and Games: Artificial Intelligence, UIN HL5627

questions.title: Shadow DCMS minister asks about timetable and industry advisory group for under-16 social media rules
questions.body: James Wild asked for the timetable for setting age-assurance requirements restricting under-16 access to social media, and whether DCMS has established an advisory group with technology companies on the forthcoming regulations. No answers are recorded in the evidence.
questions.why: Directly on online safety regulation and government engagement with technology companies on implementation.
questions.linkText: James Wild, Social Media: Children, UIN 45244

questions.title: Question on trends in spam and nuisance calls and consumer protection
questions.body: Pippa Heylings asked about trends in spam and nuisance calls to mobile phones and consumer protection. The government said Ofcom research showed the proportion of mobile users receiving suspicious calls fell from 40% in 2022 to 32% in 2026. Separately, it said the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 strengthened the enforcement regime.
questions.why: Concerns scam, spam and nuisance calls and consumer protection.

questions.title: Peer asks how government is broadening graduate routes into AI careers
questions.where: Lords written questions, Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade
questions.body: Lord Taylor of Warwick asked what steps government is taking to broaden graduate opportunities in AI-related roles. The government pointed to the up-to-£250 million TechFirst programme, including TechLocal's AI Professional Degree and Traineeship Accelerator and Spärck AI Scholarships at nine universities, plus a new Early Careers Jobs Alliance initially focused on the digital and technologies sector.
questions.why: Concerns graduate opportunities and digital/AI skills policy.
questions.linkText: Lord Taylor of Warwick, Artificial Intelligence: Graduates, UIN HL5109

other.title: Minor questions on driverless-vehicle authorisation and research funding
other.who: Mr Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi (Labour); Lord Naseby (Conservative)
other.where: Commons and Lords written questions, Department for Transport
other.body: Mr Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi asked whether overseas incidents involving a self-driving system will be considered when it is assessed for authorisation in Great Britain; no answer is recorded. Lord Naseby asked about government spending on driverless-vehicle research. The answer said there is no single government-wide estimate, but cited approximately £8 million identified by the National Audit Office for connected and autonomous vehicle research, development and innovation within the Department for Transport between 2022-23 and 2025-26.
other.why: Automated-driving regulation and public R&D spend are a minor but related thread in the wider AI-safety and automation debate.
other.linkText: Mr Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi, Driverless Vehicles, UIN 45177

today.title: Private meeting of the National Security Strategy Joint Committee
today.why: Mr Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi and Bill Esterson are listed as committee members. The evidence identifies a private meeting but supplies no agenda.

today.title: Debate on consumer subscription-contract regulations and Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act consequential amendments
today.why: The listed draft regulations concern consumer subscription-contract cancellation and information, and consequential amendments under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024.

coverage: Evidence covers Parliament up to 22 November 2026 (start of window not specified); most written answers and committee publications are dated Friday 20 November 2026.

The supplied Lords Hansard excerpts for Friday 20 November concern the Complications from Abortions (Annual Report) Bill, described in the excerpts as a Private Member's Bill. No Commons Hansard records are supplied. The supplied excerpts do not mention Microsoft, AI, cloud or data centres despite their topic tags.
No data warnings or source gaps were flagged in this evidence set.

The evidence reports 492 written questions scanned and supplies 105 written-question records. Their question and answer texts do not directly name Microsoft, Xbox, LinkedIn, Google, Amazon/AWS, OpenAI or Anthropic.
